question.prompt: Niki usually leaves her cell phone on. If her cell phone is on but she is not actually using it, the battery will last for \(24\) hours. If she is using it constantly, the battery will last for only \(3\) hours. Since the last recharge, her phone has been on \(9\) hours, and during that time she has used it for \(60\) minutes. If she doesn’t talk any more but leaves the phone on, how many more hours will the battery last?

solutions.explanation:
Measure battery charge in units equal to the charge needed for one idle hour. A full battery contains \(24\) such units. Since a full battery lasts \(3\) hours of actual use, each hour of actual use consumes \(24\div3=8\) units.

The \(60\) minutes of use equal \(1\) hour and are included in the \(9\) hours the phone has been on. Thus the phone has spent \(9-1=8\) hours idle. Its total charge consumption is
\[
8\times1+1\times8=16\text{ units}.
\]
That leaves \(24-16=8\) units. With no further talking, each remaining unit lasts one hour, so the battery will last \(8\) more hours, choice B.
solutions.title: Measure charge in idle-hour units
